analysis.one_liner: Bans paid conversion therapy as consumer fraud, with federal and state enforcement.
analysis.headline: A bill to outlaw paid conversion therapy had 43 cosponsors plus its sponsor, but the Senate Commerce Committee never acted on it and it died when that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make it a federal consumer-fraud violation for anyone to charge money for conversion therapy — practices claiming to change a person's sexual orientation or gender identity. It would let the Federal Trade Commission enforce the ban like any other deceptive-practice case, and let state attorneys general sue as well. Advertising claims that conversion therapy works or is safe would also be illegal. The bill died in committee without a hearing or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: LGBT people and their families, especially minors whose parents might pay for conversion therapy. The bill's own findings cite professional consensus that the practice has no scientific support and contributes to depression, self-harm, and suicide, so it treats paying clients as fraud victims and gives them and state enforcers a legal remedy [S2] [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Makes it unlawful for anyone to provide conversion therapy for compensation, and makes it unlawful to advertise that it will change someone's sexual orientation or gender identity or that it is harmless [S3].
Enforces the ban through the Federal Trade Commission, treating violations like other unfair or deceptive acts, with FTC penalties and rulemaking authority [S3].

Lets state attorneys general and other authorized state officials sue in federal court on behalf of their residents, and exempts support for someone undergoing gender transition and identity-exploration counseling so ordinary affirming care is untouched [S3].

Congress's stated basis: professional bodies in health, mental health, and counseling found no valid evidence conversion therapy works, and that it contributes to depression, self-harm, family rejection, and suicide [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Conversion therapy providers and any business that facilitates or profits from it, who would lose the ability to charge for the practice and face FTC and state-enforced penalties. Families currently paying for it would no longer spend money on it [S3].

drawbacks.text: Critics argue a federal ban on paid talk-based therapy raises free-speech concerns, since much conversion therapy involves speech and religious counseling; the bill itself carves out First Amendment-protected products and services, an acknowledgment of that tension [S3].

Adults who voluntarily seek counseling aimed at changing their sexual orientation would no longer be able to pay a provider for it, even as consenting adults, because the ban covers any compensated practice regardless of the client's age or consent [S3].

Some faith-based counselors contend the government should not prohibit pastoral counseling adults request, and opponents of similar state laws have argued it intrudes on religious practice; this objection is widely reported and not answered in the bill text [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protection is real and one-sided: professional health bodies have concluded the practice is ineffective and harmful, so the people paying for it are typically minors or families buying something that does not work and that major medical associations say causes harm. The honest cost is to consenting adults who want such counseling and to religious counselors who see it as their vocation, and the bill's exemption for identity-exploration and gender-transition support narrows but does not erase that collision with free-speech and religious-liberty arguments.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee on the same day, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Patty Murray introduced the Therapeutic Fraud Prevention Act of 2019 on June 27, 2019, with 32 original cosponsors [S3].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation the same day; no further action appears in the record [S5].
It gathered 43 cosponsors — 41 Democrats and 2 Independents — and none of them was a Republican [S4].
The 116th Congress ended January 3, 2021 without the committee holding a hearing, marking up the bill, or reporting it, so it never reached the Senate floor for any vote [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Paid conversion therapy providers, who faced no new federal restriction and could keep charging for the practice. Families and LGBT clients gained nothing because the ban never took effect.

industries.note: The bill would end their ability to charge for the practice and expose them to FTC and state attorney general lawsuits as fraud. Its premise is that paying clients are buying a treatment the professional consensus says does not work and causes harm.

Any organization that charges for counseling aimed at changing sexual orientation or gender identity would be covered by the ban, while the bill exempts First Amendment-protected religious products and identity-exploration or transition-support counseling, so the impact depends on how a program is structured.
